title: Minimum Window Substring
directAnswer: Find the smallest window in s that contains all characters of t (with multiplicity). The interview-grade answer is a grow-then-shrink sliding window: expand right until the window covers t, then shrink left as far as possible while it still covers t, recording the smallest valid window. Track coverage with a need-count map and a have/need formed counter. O(|s| + |t|) time, O(Σ) space.

rules: Match characters **with multiplicity** — if t = "aab", the window needs two a's.
`have` counts how many *distinct required characters* are fully satisfied; valid when `have == required`.
Increment `have` only when a count reaches exactly `need[c]` (not above).
Shrink from the left while the window is valid, recording the minimum, then break validity by dropping a needed char.
Return "" when no valid window exists (best length never updated).
whenToUse: Smallest contiguous window that covers a required multiset of items
Coverage can be tracked incrementally with a need map and a satisfied counter
Grow to become feasible, then shrink to minimize — a two-phase window
Substring/subarray 'contains all of X' minimization problems
antiSignals: Order of t matters / t must appear contiguously → that's substring search (KMP)
Longest valid window, not shortest → grow-only window (LC3, LC424)
Fixed-size window → simpler fixed sliding window (Permutation in String)
remember.takeaway: Grow-then-shrink is the template for minimum-window problems: expand the right edge until the constraint is met, then contract the left edge while it stays met. The have/need formed counter turns 'does the window cover t?' into an O(1) check per step.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can run a two-phase (grow then shrink) sliding window with character multiplicity, using a have/need formed counter to check coverage in O(1) instead of comparing maps.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Comparing the whole window map to the need map each step (O(Σ) per step), mishandling multiplicity, or incrementing `have` every time a needed char appears instead of only when its count first meets the requirement.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the brute force, then describe the grow-then-shrink window and the formed counter. Emphasize multiplicity ('aab' needs two a's) and that `have` ticks up only when a count exactly reaches the requirement.

problemStatement:
Given two strings `s` and `t` of lengths `m` and `n`, return the **minimum window substring** of `s` such that every character in `t` (**including duplicates**) is included in the window. If there is no such substring, return the empty string `""`.

The test cases are generated such that the answer is **unique**.
constraints: s and t consist of uppercase and lowercase English letters
understanding: We need the shortest contiguous slice of s that contains at least as many of each character as t requires. Multiplicity matters: covering t = "aabc" requires two a's, one b, one c. Characters not in t may also appear in the window — that's fine, we just want the smallest window that covers t.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does multiplicity matter?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. If t has two 'a's, the window must contain at least two 'a's.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the window contain extra characters not in t?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — extras are allowed; we only require that t is fully covered.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if no window covers t?
Is the answer guaranteed unique?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, the problem guarantees a unique minimal window, so we just track the smallest length.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Grow-then-shrink with a formed counter is the default; checking every substring's coverage is the brute-force baseline.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Check Every Substring
approaches.whenToMention: Say it first to anchor the baseline and to make the coverage check explicit.
hints: The answer is some substring of s. How do you check whether one substring covers all of t with multiplicity?
Build a need-count map of t. For a candidate substring, count its characters and verify each need is met.
Enumerate all O(m²) substrings, test coverage, and keep the shortest that passes. Correct but slow — the coverage recheck is the waste.
approaches.complexityReasoning: O(m²) substrings; each coverage check compares counts over the alphabet, O(Σ) (or O(window) to count). Total O(m²·Σ). The count maps are O(Σ) space.
approaches.explanation:
Precompute `need`, a count of each character in `t`. Then for every start `i` and end `j`, count the characters in `s[i..j]` and check it contains at least `need[c]` of every required `c`. Among all substrings that pass, keep the shortest.

**Why this is the natural first attempt.** It encodes the definition literally and forces you to define 'covers t' precisely: every required character appears with at least its required multiplicity. That coverage predicate is reused in the optimal solution.

**Why we don't ship this.** Enumerating all substrings and rechecking coverage from scratch is wildly redundant — adjacent windows share almost all their characters. With `m` up to `10⁵`, the quadratic (times alphabet) cost is far too slow. The optimal keeps a running window count and an O(1) coverage check, so it never recounts.
approaches.insight: Every adjacent substring differs by only one character on each end, yet the brute force recounts the entire window. Maintaining incremental counts plus a 'how many requirements are currently met' counter removes all the recounting.

pitfalls: Ignoring multiplicity — treating t as a set so "aa" passes with a single 'a'.
Rechecking full coverage every step (O(Σ)) instead of tracking it incrementally.
Forgetting the m < n early exit and the empty-string fallback.

approaches.name: Grow-Then-Shrink Window + Formed Counter (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'expand right until the window covers t, then shrink left while it still covers t, tracking the minimum'.
hints: Build need = counts of t and required = number of distinct chars in t. Keep a window count map and a counter `have` of how many distinct requirements are currently fully met.
Expand right: add s[right] to the window; if that char's window count just reached its need, increment have.

While have == required (window is valid), record the window if it's the smallest, then shrink from the left: remove s[left], and if that drops a needed char below its requirement, decrement have. Advance left.
approaches.complexityReasoning: `right` advances m times and `left` advances at most m times, each doing O(1) map work → O(m) for the scan plus O(n) to build need = O(m + n) time. The maps hold at most Σ distinct characters → O(Σ) space.
approaches.explanation:
Precompute `need` (the count of each character in `t`) and `required` (the number of *distinct* characters in `t`). Maintain a `window` count map and an integer `have` = how many distinct required characters are currently satisfied at full multiplicity. The window is valid exactly when `have == required`.

**Phase 1 — grow to feasibility.** Move `right` across `s`, incrementing `window[c]`. The instant a required character's window count *reaches* its needed count (`window[c] == need[c]`), one more requirement is met, so `have += 1`. We only bump `have` on the exact match — counting beyond the requirement doesn't satisfy a *new* requirement, so it must not increment `have` again.

**Phase 2 — shrink to minimality.** Once `have == required`, the window covers `t`. But it may be padded with junk on the left. So while it stays valid, record it if it's the smallest seen, then try to shrink: decrement `window[s[left]]` and advance `left`. If removing that character drops a *needed* character below its requirement (`window[c] < need[c]`), the window is no longer valid, so `have -= 1` and the shrink loop stops. This finds the tightest window ending at the current `right`.

**Why the formed counter beats comparing maps.** Naively you'd compare the whole window map to need at each step — O(Σ) per step. The `have`/`required` counter compresses 'is the window valid?' into a single integer comparison, updated in O(1) as characters enter and leave. That's what turns the brute force's O(m²·Σ) into O(m + n).

**Why multiplicity is handled correctly.** Because `have` increments only when a count *reaches* `need[c]` and decrements only when it *falls below* `need[c]`, a character that needs two copies contributes to `have` only while both copies are present. The window can't be declared valid with too few copies.

**Why O(m + n) time.** Each pointer sweeps `s` once; building `need` is O(n). Every character enters the window once (via `right`) and leaves at most once (via `left`).
approaches.insight: The two-phase rhythm — grow until feasible, then shrink while still feasible — is the universal minimum-window template. The reusable optimization is the `have == required` counter: rather than re-verifying the whole constraint, track *how close* you are to satisfying it and adjust by ±1 as elements cross the window boundary.

pitfalls: Incrementing have on every needed char instead of only when the count first reaches the requirement.
Comparing have against t.length() instead of the number of distinct required characters.
Decrementing have when a non-required char leaves the window (it should only react to needed chars dropping below requirement).

commonMistakes: Treating t as a set and ignoring multiplicity.
Re-verifying full coverage every step instead of using a have/required counter.
Comparing have to len(t) rather than the count of distinct required characters.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Bumping `have` past the requirement
commonMistakesDetailed.why: have must count satisfied distinct requirements. Incrementing it whenever a needed char appears (even beyond need[c]) over-counts and declares invalid windows valid.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if c in need and window[c] == need[c]:
    have += 1

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Comparing have to len(t)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: required is the number of *distinct* characters in t, not its length. For t = "aab", required is 2, not 3.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting the empty-result fallback
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If no window ever covers t, bestLen stays at its sentinel; returning a substring then throws or returns garbage.
commonMistakesDetailed.good: return "" if best_len == float('inf') else s[best_start:best_start + best_len]
